defaults.permitted_development: A straightforward internal cellar conversion in Wales can often proceed without planning permission, but external lightwells, a new separate unit, major excavation or other visible changes are likely to need it.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate basement height allowance. Any above-ground railings, boundary walls, lightwell upstands or linked external works need to be judged on their visual impact and planning status.
rules.depth_rules: There is no standalone permitted development depth right for basement excavation. The key issue is whether the works enlarge the basement or create a new basement requiring major excavation and a separate planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Basement works close to a boundary need careful review if they introduce lightwells, retaining walls, railings, drainage changes or substantial excavation near adjoining structures.
rules.roof_rules: If the project also involves a rear extension, roof terrace or roof alteration, those elements need separate assessment under the normal Welsh householder rules. A purely internal conversion does not usually create a separate roof issue.
rules.materials_rules: Visible elements such as front lightwell walls, railings, grilles, doors and paving should be designed as part of the existing house rather than as a bolt-on intervention. Heritage settings usually need the most restrained detailing.

rules.permitted_development: The easiest Welsh basement case is an internal conversion within the existing space. A new basement, new lightwell, separate accommodation or material external change is much more likely to need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Height only becomes an issue where the basement scheme creates visible above-ground elements. Railings, retaining walls, lightwell upstands and other external additions are usually the parts that need checking.
rules.depth_rules: Basement works in Wales do not benefit from an automatic excavation right. Once the proposal digs a new basement or materially extends the underground floorplate, expect a distinct planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: The planning question is usually hardest at the boundary, especially if the proposal adds lightwells, railings, retaining walls or major excavation next to adjoining property. Neighbour and structural impacts often sit alongside the formal application route.
rules.roof_rules: The roof is rarely the deciding issue for a purely internal basement conversion. It becomes relevant only where the overall scheme includes roof alterations or other visible above-ground work.
rules.materials_rules: Where the basement proposal introduces visible external work, keep the materials quiet and well integrated with the dwelling. Front lightwell details, railings and entrance alterations usually need the most careful design.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Wales, conservation area controls and any Article 4 direction can remove normal householder permitted development rights for visible external work. Check the planning register before relying on national allowances.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be needed for internal or external works that affect the character of a listed building or its curtilage structures. Minor-looking changes can still need consent in Wales.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: In Wales, an existing basement or cellar can often be converted internally without planning permission where the use is not significantly changed and the outside is left alone. New excavation, a lightwell or a separate unit usually changes that position.

rules.height_rules: Basement projects are not governed by a simple height cap in Wales. The practical question is whether any above-ground parts such as lightwell walls, guard rails or altered entrances materially change the outside appearance.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is often the core basement question, but Wales does not give a simple dig-down allowance. Creating new underground volume or materially enlarging the basement usually needs separate planning review.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary conditions matter most where the scheme cuts new lightwells, alters retaining structures or excavates close to neighbouring buildings. Planning, drainage and structural issues often have to be worked through together.
rules.roof_rules: A basement conversion does not usually raise its own roof question unless the wider project adds terraces, rooflights, plant or linked above-ground alterations. Those elements must be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: Most material concerns arise only where the scheme changes what you can see from outside. Lightwell linings, guard rails, paving and new joinery should be detailed as part of the host property rather than an obvious add-on.

rules.permitted_development: In Wales, an existing basement or cellar can often be converted internally without planning permission where the use is not significantly changed and the outside is left alone. New excavation, a lightwell or a separate unit usually changes that position.

rules.height_rules: Basement projects are not governed by a simple height cap in Wales. The practical question is whether any above-ground parts such as lightwell walls, guard rails or altered entrances materially change the outside appearance.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is often the core basement question, but Wales does not give a simple dig-down allowance. Creating new underground volume or materially enlarging the basement usually needs separate planning review.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary conditions matter most where the scheme cuts new lightwells, alters retaining structures or excavates close to neighbouring buildings. Planning, drainage and structural issues often have to be worked through together.
rules.roof_rules: A basement conversion does not usually raise its own roof question unless the wider project adds terraces, rooflights, plant or linked above-ground alterations. Those elements must be assessed separately.

rules.permitted_development: The easiest Welsh basement case is an internal conversion within the existing space. A new basement, new lightwell, separate accommodation or material external change is much more likely to need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Height only becomes an issue where the basement scheme creates visible above-ground elements. Railings, retaining walls, lightwell upstands and other external additions are usually the parts that need checking.
rules.depth_rules: Basement works in Wales do not benefit from an automatic excavation right. Once the proposal digs a new basement or materially extends the underground floorplate, expect a distinct planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: The planning question is usually hardest at the boundary, especially if the proposal adds lightwells, railings, retaining walls or major excavation next to adjoining property. Neighbour and structural impacts often sit alongside the formal application route.
rules.roof_rules: The roof is rarely the deciding issue for a purely internal basement conversion. It becomes relevant only where the overall scheme includes roof alterations or other visible above-ground work.
rules.materials_rules: Where the basement proposal introduces visible external work, keep the materials quiet and well integrated with the dwelling. Front lightwell details, railings and entrance alterations usually need the most careful design.
